doc.title: Grover Mitchell interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, February 13, 1996

title: Basie reshaping arrangements: 'L'il Darling' and vaudeville piano
summary: Basie slowed Neal Hefti's 'L'il Darling', and his sparse piano came from accompanying vaudeville dancers; arrangers saw their work turned around.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Basie had a way of tailoring arrangements to feature his sound?
Yeah. What he did, a good example of that was “L’il Darling.” When Neal brought “L’il Darling” in it was supposed to be fast. Did you know that?

[scats]. And Basie says, “it’s a nice song but it’s terrible,” and he slowed it way back [scats]. And there was a couple of more he did that way. And he could do just the opposite with something that was maybe would play faster. He was very good at tempo. Now you see he came through that Vaudeville school you know with the dancers and all that kind of stuff, and he had really good insight. A lot of that sparse piano style of his came from accompanying dancers. If you could remember how piano players used to accompany tap dancers. So you see what I mean, it was just a removal from that, and taking advantage of this real sparse musical type of thing with the band. If you could imagine a piano player that had to accompany tap dancers, Basie was a perfect example of that. That’s how that little plink here and a plink there got to be part of, well to a great degree it got to be part of what he was doing. He was a Vaudevillian.
That must have been quite an experience for an arranger to work on something and keep hearing this — here’s how it goes in my head — to come in and he’d say, “no, not like that.”
